name: Agent: Email Development
summary: Turns a Figma design into an email that looks right in every inbox — including the ones that break everything.
objectives: Turn a Figma design into an email that looks right in every inbox — including the ones that break everything.
Stop a broken email before it sends, with a check that runs as code instead of a person squinting at it.

outcomes.text: Anyone can download the agent and build an email with it. There is a guide that walks through it, step by step.

The inboxes that break the most — Outlook on Windows, Outlook.com, Gmail in dark mode — now each have a recipe that works, tested on real renders. Every attempt is written down, including the ones that failed and the limits still being lived with.

evidence.label: Dark mode: what worked, what didn't

outcomes.text: The pre-send checklist runs as code. It reads the finished email, stops the send if a rule is broken, and writes up what it found.

evidence.label: The check that blocks a bad send

outcomes.text: Design to email is a written ten-step process, not one person's habit — so a second person gets the same result as the first.

It built a whole newsletter for a brand it had never seen — different colours, a different font, a different language and layout — from its generic rules alone. It passed, and the two gaps that showed up became new rules.
One email pipeline instead of two. The old system was retired and the agent's template became the only source of real email, so nobody has to ask which of the two is right.

An independent check went looking for holes in the agent — twice. One reader had its rules and asked whether it does what it says; a second was given only the code and asked whether what it says is right. Thirty-six findings between them, only two found by both.

Three of the thirty-six could send a wrong email — the sharpest let an advisor's photo come from a default row while their name did not, so one person's name could go out over another's face. All three are fixed, each checked by re-running the exact failure reported.

The blind read also exposed a limit in the method: this agent is almost entirely written rules, and hiding the rules from that reader hides most of the agent with them. So twenty-six of the thirty-six findings are about the example project. Only ten are about the agent itself.

All thirty-six are closed. The ones that mattered were not broken code but confident sentences: a rule telling you to do what the checker forbids, and two items marked "checked automatically" that nothing checked. A program now reads the agent's own documents and fails when they drift.

The generator used to finish green after failing — an error, a lost email, a broken link, and it still reported success. It now stops and says which row and why, and checks the emails that actually get sent rather than only a fixed sample. The safety net went from 13 automated checks to 160.

Last round's fixes were re-tested one at a time, by re-running the exact failure each one originally reported — not by reading the write-up that claimed they were fixed. Twelve of the thirteen about the agent itself genuinely hold.

The thirteenth is open on purpose: whether the unsubscribe line reaches the reader cannot be answered until the first real send. The agent now prints that reminder at the end of every production run, so it fires when someone can act on it.

The same round found seven more. The sharpest is a check written during the last round of fixes: it reports that it examined every file that travels, and it examines seven of twelve. A rule-breaking line in either file anyone downloads passes it clean.

Four of the seven sit in work the last round of fixes produced — which is why a session that fixes findings never grades its own. The agent and the example project inside it are now checked as two subjects: a flaw in the example cannot follow anyone who copies the agent.

A third reader went over the agent again, with no sight of what the previous one had found, and reported thirteen more. The two that could send a wrong email are not broken code at all — each exists only between two documents that disagree.

Three pages require every block to carry its own background colour "without exception". A fourth forbids exactly that inside one Outlook construction, and a real-inbox test had already proved the version the other three demand is the one that breaks.

The pre-send checklist likewise demands a fallback font the agent's own first page forbids for any brand whose typeface has serifs. Following the checklist produces the mistake that page exists to prevent.

Checking this agent blind is not possible the usual way, and the round measured that instead of assuming it: hide the written rules and only three of its eighteen files are the agent. The rules were reviewed directly, and the report states what that cannot prove.

A third session merged the two readings, seeing only the two lists and never the agent itself: sixteen findings, five of them able to send a wrong email or break a promise the agent makes about itself. Five were caught by both readers; eleven by only one.

Four of those five came from the reader kept blind to everything already answered. None is broken code — each lives between two documents that disagree, exactly where a reader who knew the history had stopped looking.

The round also priced its own blind spot rather than hiding it: nobody read the code without knowing what it was meant to do. Faults where the code and the rules agree with each other and both are wrong about the world went uncovered by design, and the report says so.

All sixteen findings are fixed, one change per finding. Each fix was proved by re-running the exact failure it was reported against, and each new automatic check by deliberately breaking what it is meant to catch — because this round found two checks reporting success while examining nothing.

The worst was one of those: a check reporting it covered every file that travels covered seven of twelve, measuring itself against that same short list. A rule-breaking line planted in either file anyone downloads passed it clean. The count now comes from the folder.

The send checker also under-enforced its own promise. It claimed to stop any unfilled placeholder and quietly ignored every one containing a digit, so a half-finished email could go out with the check green and the box ticked.

Three contradictions between documents were resolved in favour of the page proved right in a real inbox, and each is now held together by a program: where a rule has an exception, every page stating the rule must state the exception too.

The commands in the last step before a real send did not work from any directory — the checker sits in one place and the files it checks in another. They now say where to run them from, and a program refuses a command that cannot find its own script.

The write-up of this round does not grade itself. It lists what changed, what each change newly exposed, and twelve starting points for the next reading — including one the fixes uncovered: the agent’s own checker cannot pass on the stripped-down copy the agent says it hands out.
The public copy anyone can download is the fixed one again: all nine published files match the source exactly, and the internal record, the client project and the maintainer tooling stayed out of it.

A third check went over the agent, and it is the last one. Three rounds is now a deliberate limit: on a sister project the same checking ran seven times and each round found more than the one before, because every round ended up reading the paperwork the previous one had produced.
Twelve findings. Three of them could send a wrong email, and all three are fixed.

The sharpest was two programs making the same mistake and agreeing with each other. One adds a marker to the finished email so the Gmail dark-mode fix can work; the other confirms the marker is there. Both looked for that marker the same wrong way.

So on an email carrying a similarly-named setting, the marker was never added, that unrelated setting was quietly overwritten, and both programs reported success. The Gmail dark-mode fix silently did nothing, and nothing anywhere said so.

The check for Outlook's rounded buttons could never fail on the emails it exists for: it was satisfied by text inside a comment, which is exactly where the agent's own example puts it. It also failed every email with no rounded buttons, demanding something they have no use for.

Two pages promised that a real send cannot go out unchecked. Only the example project keeps that promise, and the agent ships without it — so anyone copying the agent got the sentence and not the mechanism. Both pages now say whose job it is, and a program holds them to it.

Every fix was proved by deleting it again and confirming a test fails. The tool refuses to report anything at all if the deletion did not actually apply — the exact failure that let three fixes on a sister project be recorded as proved when nothing had been tested.

That refusal caught one of this round's own fixes straight away: a safety net that cannot be reached while the code around it is correct, so no test could show it worked. It is now proved by deliberately breaking the code it guards.

The other nine findings are written down as a backlog instead of becoming more work. They get fixed when someone is next in those files for a real product reason. A backlog drained by a session of its own is just another round of checking under a different name.

The round also priced itself: the two independent readers agreed on one finding out of twelve. Reading the agent twice is now something you opt into before shipping it or handing it to someone else, rather than the default — it extends the list more than it confirms it.
The copy anyone can download carries the third round's fixes. All nine published files were checked one by one against the source and match exactly — five changed, four were already identical.

That check was done on what the site actually serves, not on a local copy, because a republish is a manual step and the gap between "I pushed it" and "it is there" is exactly where a stale claim hides.

The two scripts were also run together inside the published copy, not only in the source tree. One of the fixes made them depend on each other for the first time, and the download is the only place that dependency could quietly fail.

milestones.title: Put everything the team knew about email into one portable set of rules
Retire the old system, so there is one pipeline instead of two
Make the agent's template the only source of real email
Turn the pre-send checklist into code that blocks a bad send
Prove it end to end and turn production back on
Prove it works for a brand it has never seen
Publish the agent and its guide, so anyone can use it
Give the team a way to draft and check an email without running code
Have the agent independently checked twice — once against its own rules, once by a reader who never saw them
Fix everything the two checks found, and prove each fix against the original failure
Check a second time whether the fixes held, and look again for what the first pass missed
Fix what the second round found, and prove each fix against the original failure
Republish the public copy of the agent, so what anyone can download is the fixed one
Check the agent a third and final time, fix everything that could send a wrong email, and close it to further checking
Republish the public copy again, so what anyone can download includes the third round's fixes
